inline.s: Mr. Shen was by nature strong and vigorous, and he repeatedly committed adultery. Wang Xing'an once warned him, saying: “If I violate another man's wife, another man will violate mine. The retribution is fearsome. You would do well to mend your ways a little.” Shen laughed and said: “Have you ever seen a man fond of beauty become a cuckold? I keep my women's quarters strictly shut; what is there to worry about?” One day he came home from outside and saw with his own eyes his wife coupling naked with another man. He wanted to seize a weapon and strike them, but his hand could not be raised. His wife, thinking her husband would not make an issue of it, took her pleasure with the man at leisure. Shen, in a fury, glared, stamped his feet, heaved one deep sigh, and died.

A certain man had done evil all his life. One close to him was lodging in his house by night when he heard two voices speaking: “So-and-so's wickedness is full to overflowing; he must receive retribution.” One asked, “Shall he have his line cut off?” The answer came, “Too heavy.” “Shall he suffer fire?” “Too light.” “Wang Xiaoxiao.” “Enough, enough.” The hearer was astonished and could not make out the reason. Some years later the man became infatuated with a courtesan, this Wang Xiaoxiao, and married her and brought her home. He listened to her words and followed her counsel; she estranged his own flesh and blood, and when his wealth was utterly exhausted, he died.

The monk Xingyun saw a lotus blossom sway and suddenly gave rise to a lustful thought. That night a woman knocked at his door. Xingyun opened it and saw a maiden with a maidservant, who called herself Lady Lotus, her face and figure bright enough to dazzle a man. Xingyun was overjoyed and dallied and talked with her. In a moment the lamp went out. The attendant heard Xingyun crying out in pain. The woman said in a stern voice: “Why did you rashly give rise to a lustful heart? Even if I were truly a woman, would I be willing to lie with you illicitly?” The attendant ran to tell the monks, and they pushed open the door and entered. What they saw was two yakṣas. Xingyun's head was already parted from his body.

This compilation sets out one after another the cases of calamity brought by lust, and it places the case of the scholar of Guixi first precisely in order to make plain the subtle meaning of the Most High's words, “when the thought arises, it is a private act”: to urge men to be cautious and reverent at the very beginning, in the moment when the eye sees and the mind stirs, and to take pains to be careful there. And this case of Xingyun is not even a matter of the mind stirring at the sight of beauty; it is without head or brain, the mind conjuring up images, building a tower where there is no mirage, holding a market where there is no sea, secretly and darkly fashioning evil, boring its own chaos open — until at last the yakṣas devour him and his head is parted from his body. Wicked demons and monstrous calamities, cruel and ghastly to this degree. Reading this case, who would not tremble in heart and shudder in liver? Therefore I make it the conclusion; there is deep meaning in this. Think on it, think on it.

Lin Maoxian of Xinzhou was a man of great talent, and he was recommended for the provincial examination. His family was poor, so he shut his door and studied. A neighbor girl, whose own husband did not study, admired Maoxian's fame for talent and came to him by night. Maoxian rebuked her, saying: “Man and woman must keep their separate places; the rites and the law do not permit it. Heaven and earth, the gods and the spirits, are ranged and spread all around us. How could you defile me?” The girl withdrew in shame. The next year Maoxian passed the examination, and afterward all three of his sons passed as well.

Yao Sanjiu was originally surnamed Bian, a man of wide learning and skilled in poetry and prose, and he taught in the house of the Huai family. A daughter of the house often came spying on him; Bian sat stern and upright and paid her no heed. One day he set his shoes out to dry in the courtyard, and the girl wrote a letter and slipped it into his shoe. Bian found it and made some other excuse to take his leave and go home. Yuan Yixing wrote a poem in praise of him, with the lines: “One speck of chastity, firm as no stone; / let not the spring wind and peach and plum suspect each other.” Bian would not accept the poem, and moreover answered with a letter insisting that there had been no such thing. Yixing sealed up his letter and wrote on it: “Virtue is most abundant; his sons and grandsons will surely flourish.” Later his son Chen and his great-grandson Xi both passed the imperial examination.

In his youth Tang Gao was reading by his lamp when a woman teased him and poked a hole through the paper window. Tang Gao mended it and wrote a poem on it, saying: “A paper window poked through is easy to mend; / it is hardest to repair the hidden virtue one has harmed.” One evening a monk passed his gate and saw a plaque reading “Number One Scholar,” with two lanterns hung to left and right, and on them were just these two lines. Astonished, the monk questioned him about it. In the end he indeed came first in the whole empire.

Wang Tianyu met a man of strange powers who read his face and said: “Your features resemble those of an arhat, but you will lack heirs, and your life will not be long.” Thereupon Wang made light of wealth and delighted in giving. One day, lodging at Qingjiangpu, his young and pretty hostess came to him of her own accord. Wang shut the door and would not admit her, saying: “How could I ruin your reputation and your chastity?” The woman went away ashamed. Later he met the physiognomist again, who said: “What hidden virtue have you done? Your features have suddenly changed. You ought to have a noble son, and to live past eighty.” In the end it was as he said. Looking over the sages of old who turned away women who came running to them, some drew their strength from the word “forbearance” — “what you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.” Some feared to damage their hidden merit, dreading only that their blessings would be cut short and their years shortened. Their learning may have differed, yet all alike accorded with the uprightness of heavenly principle and the peace of the human heart; it is the way by which both self and other are kept whole. At such a moment, when blessing comes, the mind grows quick: one already seems to have climbed serenely into the blue clouds, and does not wait for the reward before rejoicing. In sum, the ways of turning away women who come running are not one; one must know them all in advance in careful detail, and only then will one not be confused when the matter arrives. There are many, indeed, who by a stern countenance and a sharp rebuke send her away at once. But there are also those who refuse and she still will not go, like Lu Rong, who pleaded that his illness was not yet healed and agreed to a meeting a few nights later — both are fit models. Or one may open the door and go out: thus Cao Fen went to lodge elsewhere, the quick response of a man of complete virtue. There are also those who swear to die: thus Mao Lumen refused the maidservant who came running to him, and when she said, “If so, then I have only death,” Lumen was not moved. There are those who refuse her all night and she is still there, like Doctor Chen — “I cannot, I cannot” — who then pushed open the window and stood exposed in the courtyard, vowing to do nothing base. And there is the man who firmly declined a gift of a hundred pieces of gold and still refused her sternly — such pure virtue and resolute decision is truly fit to be a model. If the door is already shut and the woman is outside, the door must not be opened. If in the morning one makes an excuse and takes leave to go home and she still summons one, one must not come again. Yet one must never speak of it in all one's life; even one's wife and children should not be told of the matter. Only this is abundant virtue. From this one ascends to be first in the empire, attains high position, brings glory to one's forebears, and prolongs one's line. Compared with piling up merit along other roads, the difference in difficulty is ten thousand times over.

In Zhejiang there was a certain commandant who engaged a tutor to instruct his son. The tutor fell ill with a cold and wished to bring on a sweat, so he had the boy fetch him a quilt. By mistake the boy rolled up one of his mother's shoes in it. When the illness was over and the quilt was returned, the shoe fell out beside the mat; neither the tutor nor the boy knew of it. The commandant saw it and suspected his wife of an intrigue. She would not submit, so he sent a maidservant to invite the tutor in his wife's name by a ruse. The tutor angrily rebuked the maid. The commandant then forced his wife to go in person, while he himself held a bare blade and waited for the door to open. The tutor firmly refused, saying: “I was invited here by my host; how could I fall into secret misconduct? I swear I will never open this door.” In the morning the tutor took his leave. The commandant said: “Sir, you are truly a gentleman,” and told him the whole story and begged him to stay. That examination season the tutor passed.

Cheng Yanbin attacked the city of Ning. On the day the city fell, his attendants presented him with three virgins, all of uncommon beauty. He was drunk at the time, and said to the girls: “You are as my own daughters; how would I dare violate you?” He sealed them into a room by himself, and at dawn he sought out their parents and returned them. Afterward he rose to the office of inspector, and at the age of ninety-three he took leave of family and friends and passed away. All his sons became eminent.

Xu Xi of Jiangyin in the Ming dynasty was, when he was a clerk in the military office, involved in a case where men were taken for garrison duty in distant lands and a strong man was drafted. By mistake this fell upon one man, who could not clear himself and wished to beg Xu Xi to release him. His family was poor, but his wife was young and beautiful, so he set out wine for Xu Xi and had his wife drink with him. Presently the man made an excuse and left. Xu Xi hurried out, but the wife, afraid that Xu Xi would go and ruin the matter, caught at his robe to keep him and told him her husband's intention. Xu Xi refused her sternly, tore his robe free, and fled. The next day he reproved her husband severely, and in the end cleared him. Afterward Xu Xi rose in office to be Minister of War.

Zhang Wenqi of Fujian and a certain Zhou fled from bandits into a mountain cave. A beautiful woman was already there before them. Seeing the men arrive, she fled in panic. Zhang said: “If you go, you will surely meet the bandits. We are honest and careful men; we too have come here to escape the bandits, and would never dare violate you.” In the middle of the night Zhou repeatedly tried to assault her, and Zhang restrained him with all his strength. At dawn Zhang and Zhou left the cave to look for news, meaning to draw Zhou out with him and leave the woman in peace. Once out of the mountains they learned the bandits had withdrawn, so they came back to the cave with a village elder, who asked after the woman's parents, her native place, and her surname. Zhang urgently had the elder escort her home. Not long after, a certain Mr. Huang prepared a generous dowry and took Zhang as his son-in-law: it was the woman who had taken refuge from the bandits. Her father, moved by Zhang's virtue, gave her to him in marriage. Afterward both of Zhang's sons passed the examinations.

Mr. Chen of Yugan was skilled in medicine. A poor scholar fell ill with a wasting disease and was near death; Chen treated him and cured him, and did not demand payment. Later Chen passed by his house at dusk and was pressed to stay the night. The mother-in-law said to her daughter-in-law: “Your husband owes his life to that man. Why do you not share his bed to repay him?” The wife murmured assent. That night she came to him. Chen refused her, saying: “What of your mother-in-law?” The wife said: “This was my mother-in-law's own wish.” He said: “What of your husband?” She said: “My husband's body was your gift; what claim has he on me?” Chen said: “I cannot.” She pressed him, and Chen said again and again: “I cannot, I cannot.” So he sat until dawn, and taking up a brush wrote the words “I cannot” over and over on the desk. Afterward, when he could barely hold himself in check, he cried out aloud: “These two words, I cannot — they are very hard.” Then he pushed open the window and stood exposed in the courtyard, and went away only at daybreak. Later, when Chen's son entered the examinations, the chief examiner threw out his paper. Suddenly he heard a voice call: “You cannot.” He read it again and again threw it out, and again heard the voice cry repeatedly: “You cannot, you cannot.” The last time he read it, he had resolved to throw it out, when suddenly he heard a loud voice cry: “These two words, I cannot — they are very hard,” and the cry would not stop. The examiner therefore passed him, and afterward he became a presented scholar. All the above are cases of a heart set on uprightness and free of private desire. But there is no way to deal with one in whom principle and desire are locked in battle. So I set out this case of one who held firm on the verge of chaos, to show the method.

Qi Wang of Jinhua was fifty and had no son. A physiognomist said: “You have an evil air about you; you must have something on your conscience.” Qi Wang said: “In my youth I once violated a woman in her inner chamber.” The physiognomist said in alarm: “For that offense a man's sons and grandsons ought to be cut off. Of all evils, lust is the hardest to repent. Some great good is needed before Heaven's mind can be turned back.” Qi Wang therefore reformed. In the first year, he rejoiced in giving and was never stingy when men proposed good works. The physiognomist said: “Not yet.” In the second year, whenever he met with a good work hard to perform, he was first to contribute more than half. The physiognomist said: “Not yet.” In the third year, he carried out good works single-handed and would not yield precedence to others. The physiognomist said: “The lines of hidden merit have appeared; why worry that you will have no son?” In the end he had a son. At seventy Qi Wang was still able to hold his grandson in his arms.

Lu Qing of the Ming dynasty loved to talk of lewdness and to peep at women. At thirty he was utterly poor, and two sons died one after the other. One day he suddenly died, and saw his grandfather, who said in anger: “Our two generations piled up goodness; the retribution due you was a vast fortune. Who would have thought your heart would love lust and your mouth and eyes create sin, so that your blessings were all but cut away? I feared you would again commit the actual evil of lust, and that your descendants would be utterly without hope, so I earnestly begged the King of the Underworld to summon you here for a look, that you might know the gain and loss.” Lu Qing said: “I have heard that violating another man's wife or daughter brings the retribution of no descendants, and I truly feared that; I never committed it.” An official beside them said: “Is it only the cutting off of descendants? If a woman comes to seduce you and you do not refuse her, then you are only repaid with no descendants. But as for those who lure and coerce, and those who offend again and again, those who ruin relations, those who procure abortions, those who kill husbands — what crimes are those? Is it only the cutting off of descendants? The yang law is lenient toward lustful evil; the yin law is strictest of all. Whenever a man stirs a single thought of desire, the three corpse-spirits report it of themselves, and the Kitchen God and the City God petition on high; to conceal or omit any part of it is a grave fault. Only watch today's sentencing and you will know.” In a little while the ghost attendants brought in a crowd of lustful offenders, cangue-laden and kneeling. The King of the Underworld gave his orders in a stern voice, saying: “So-and-so is to become a beggar, mad and mute. So-and-so is to become a prostitute, blind. So-and-so is to be an ox for two lives. So-and-so is to be a pig for ten lives.” All were led out by the ghost attendants to be reborn. Lu Qing's hair stood on end and his marrow froze. The official said: “There are things worse even than these. Do not covet half a moment of pleasure and lose this human body. You should shun beauty as you would an arrow, and carve these words to admonish the world.” Afterward the King of the Underworld released Lu Qing to return. Lu Qing carved and printed the Record of a Journey Through the Underworld, printing ten thousand copies to awaken the world. He did good with all his strength. At forty he had two sons in succession and raised a fortune of ten thousand in gold. Then he cut off all worldly ties and went to the Southern Sea to cultivate the Way. Cai Jing, a man of his own village, wrote it down. The two cases above, the good reward of repentance for lust, are set out here in order to make firm the repentant heart of those who have already stumbled. For this is the way to turn calamity into blessing. Alas! The one evil of lust — the brush can hardly exhaust it, and how could speech ever come to its end? I can only daily hope that the wise and the foolish, those who have not yet offended and those already stained, will each and all think deeply on it, and that their heavenly conscience may come to light early.

Goods are vessels and implements; wealth is silver and money; to be in debt means to have borrowed them in a time of need to tide oneself over, and then, after a long while, to be ungrateful and not repay. The Scripture of Admonitions says: “If you owe another a debt and for the moment have nothing with which to make it good, think long and anxiously of the debt, and diligently consider how to repay it.” If because one has not repaid it, one instead wishes that the creditor might die and so wipe out the trace of it, such a mind as this is a jackal and a wolf in this present life, and how could it escape becoming dog or horse in the life to come? It is foolishness indeed.

Bai Yuantong owed Yang Yun four thousand five hundred cash and, though pressed again and again, did not repay it. When Yang Yun died, he simply concealed the matter. Later the Yang family had a donkey born to them, which suddenly spoke in human speech, saying: “I am Bai Yuantong. Because I owed you four thousand five hundred cash, I have come to this. Now the donkey-selling family in the Western Market likewise owes money to me, exactly this sum. Sell me to them quickly, and take the price to repay yourselves, and the debt will be settled.” Yang's son did as he said; two days after the sale the donkey died.

Yan Chang of the Han dynasty was a commandery officer. The governor Diwu Chang was once summoned to court, and entrusted to Yan Chang a hundred and thirty thousand cash of his salary, which Yan Chang buried. Later, when Diwu Chang was dying, he summoned his orphaned grandson of nine and said to him: “I have thirty thousand cash left with the officer Yan Chang.” When the grandson grew up he sought out Yan Chang, who was both grieved and glad to see him, and at once took out the money and returned it, the seals and markings just as they had been. The grandson said: “My grandfather said only thirty thousand; now it is a hundred and thirty thousand. I dare not take it.” Yan Chang said: “The governor, sick and confused, spoke in error. Have no doubt, young sir.” In the end he returned it all. Yan Chang afterward rose to be provincial governor.

To solicit means every matter great and small; whoever begs or entreats or asks a favor of another, all of it is this. Not to succeed means not to get one's wish. To curse is to wish calamity upon him; to hate is to store up resentment and venom. The noble man understands principle and rests content in his lot; how could he be willing to solicit from others? If perchance he does so, he is already no upright man. And if he does not succeed, he should only turn and examine himself. If he goes further and curses and hates, then he is truly a petty man who turns and turns again.

In the Song dynasty a certain Lu went by night carrying a hundred pieces of gold to Wang Dan, asking to be made transport commissioner for the Huai and Yangtze region. The duke declined, saying: “Your talents are not equal to this office. How would I dare set public matters aside for private favor?” Lu withdrew in shame, and all night long burned incense and cursed, wishing Wang Dan a speedy death. In a dream a god rebuked him, saying: “Wang is loyal in heart to the state, and you wish him a speedy death. The Emperor of Heaven will bring the guilt home to you.” Indeed, within a few days Lu died.

Li Geng of Hangzhou in the Ming dynasty was poor and of no principle. From all his relatives and neighbors he went about begging loans, and if he met the least refusal he fell into unending rage and hatred. One day he asked a friend for grain, and when the friend would not consent, Li Geng at once cursed him before the god, wishing him a speedy death. In a moment there was a crash of thunder, and Li Geng fell dead before the god.

Yu Tieqiao said: In soliciting from others, my own feelings may be most urgent, but of the men from whom one solicits, some are without the means and some are constrained by circumstance, so that nine in ten appeals fail and one in ten succeeds. This is the ordinary way of things. If one rashly gives rise to curses and hatred, will the other man, because of my curses and hatred, suddenly turn about and pity me? One only adds to the obstruction of one's own afflictions. Such a man not only does not know the decree of Heaven; he also does not understand the ways of the world.

Xie Liangzuo of the Song dynasty said: In all things there is in truth a decree; human calculation cannot contend with it. In all my life I have never solicited from others, and my letters have never reached those in power. When someone urged me to do so, I answered: “How could he promote me? I have my own decree.” Fan Zhongxuan of the Song dynasty said: “Though a man be utterly foolish, in reproving others he is clear-sighted; though a man be utterly clear-sighted, in forgiving himself he is blind. If a man can reprove himself with the heart with which he reproves others, and forgive others with the heart with which he forgives himself, the station of sage and worthy — there is no fear he will not reach it.” Whoever solicits from others and lays blame on them should repeat these two gentlemen's words three times over.

To lose one's opportunity means to meet with a matter that cannot be done and to find oneself in circumstances where one cannot get one's way. In the affairs and circumstances of this world, ruin is easy and success is hard, and the adverse outnumber the favorable. One may have an unlucky fate and an unpropitious time, so that whatever one does is thrown into confusion; or one may by a chance error go wrong and find it too late to repent. The hardship of the road is the same lament in every age. Yet there is a kind of man who is not near to human feeling: in ordinary days he loves to make a show of friendship, but once trouble and defeat come he always places himself outside the game and laughs at the man whose elbows are being pulled, saying: “It was his own fault in the first place.” Alas! Let him examine his own life in turn: has he truly never once done a single thing amiss?

Wang Sheng of Hanzhou in the Ming dynasty loved to point out other men's faults. A neighbor of his had lost a son, and Wang Sheng upbraided him, saying: “It is because your wickedness is extreme that you have this retribution.” Not long after, Wang Sheng's own two sons both died of illness, and the neighbor mocked him in turn, saying: “I suppose your wickedness must be even more extreme.” Again, when a cousin of his clan sat for the annual examination and was placed in the fourth rank, Wang Sheng pointed at him too, saying: “His writing is truly absurd; how could he hope for a high place?” Within a year, in the provincial examination Wang Sheng himself was placed in the fifth rank, and his cousin mocked him in turn, saying: “I suppose my cousin's writing is even more absurd.”

Guan Zhong said: “I once planned affairs together with Bao Shu, and instead met with deeper poverty and hardship; Bao Shu did not think me foolish, knowing that time may be favorable or unfavorable. I was three times an official and three times driven out by my lord; Bao Shu did not think me unworthy, knowing that I had not met my time.” From this we may see that the great men of old, too, often had their lost opportunities. What is precious is a man who understands one, to comfort and encourage one in the midst of poverty and hardship. How could one, because his steps have once gone astray, go on to drop stones upon him? Such a man has lost the duty of compassion and has turned his back on the benevolence of lending a hand; he delights in calamity and rejoices in disaster, and is neither benevolent nor wise. Calamity will surely overtake his own person.

A body maimed in its four limbs, a form and feature coarse and mean — these come either from evil karma in a former life or from the misfortunes visited upon one by one's parents. When one meets such people, one ought to pity them and keep them whole; how could one bear to mock them? And moreover a man's accomplishment lies in his capacity and discernment, not in his bodily form. Zhou Bo, though he stammered, became a minister; Yan Ying, though small of body, brought his lord to prominence. These are recorded in the histories and cannot be numbered. And since men whose bodies are incomplete often hate themselves for it, to mock them is to tread upon what they most resent. The mother of Duke Qing of Qi laughed at Que Ke and was attacked. The beauty of the Lord of Pingyuan laughed at a lame man and was put to death. The people of Zhao mocked Lord Mengchang as a little man and were killed. All these are overturned carts before us, and may serve as deep warnings.

The Buddhist scriptures speak of the fruit that flows on evenly from like to like, meaning that when a man lives in the world with a mind and craft not upright, then in life after life to come his bodily form will be incomplete, his mouth and eyes askew, his four limbs maimed and lacking. This says that karma made in a former life is the cause of the incomplete body and form one receives in this life. If so, then when a man is at the very point of giving rise to a thought, in the subtle stirring of a single motion of mind, may he not be warned, cautious, and in fear, lest he drift into what is crooked and perverse?

The Essential Summary of the Daoist Canon says: The prohibitions concerning the bedchamber are many, and those concerning thunder are the most severe of all. The Monthly Ordinances says: Three days before the first thunder, the wooden clapper is sounded to proclaim to the myriad people: “Thunder is about to sound. Those who do not keep watch over their bearing and conduct will bear children incomplete, and calamity will surely follow.” This is because they profane the majesty of Heaven. Here it speaks of parents who are not careful, and so bring it about that their children's bodies are incomplete.

Lu Qi of the Tang dynasty had a face the color of indigo. When Guo Ziyi fell ill, the hundred officials came in throngs to inquire after him, and his concubines and attendants filled the room before him, nor did he ever send them out. But when Lu Qi arrived, he had them all withdrawn. Someone asked him why, and Guo Ziyi said: “His face is ugly and his heart is treacherous. If the women see him they will surely laugh, and one day when he gains power, not one of my clan will be left alive.” Later Lu Qi became prime minister, and took revenge for the smallest glance; only the Guo family alone came through unscathed.

Hou Yuan'gong was very poor in appearance. When he first drank at the provincial banquet, men did not respect him because he was advanced in years and ugly. Some frivolous fellows painted Yuan'gong's likeness on a paper kite and let it fly on a string. Yuan'gong saw it and laughed, and wrote on it: “Unmet, in hiding, who would trust my worth? / Only now my name and trace appear. / For no cause the skillful craftsman paints my form; / I borrow the wind lightly, and with one lift mount the empty sky. / Barely does the breeze lift me and my body steady grows; / I almost doubt I journey far to the moon palace. / After the rain the evening sun is red. / How many men on level ground / Look up and see me among the purple clouds?” That year he passed the examination and rose to the office of prime minister. The boys of his home village were all too ashamed to face him.

Yu Tieqiao said: A man's body and form are by nature nothing to rely on. The crippled, the sick, the maimed, the disabled — none of these can be known in advance. A beautiful eye may be pierced and blinded; a swift foot may be broken and lamed. “From now on I know how to escape this” — how fraught with peril were those words of Zengzi! If one has not even time enough to love oneself, how dare one laugh at others? Those who make up nicknames, compose songs and rhymes, and sketch and mock at others — let them take this to heart and change their evil habits once for all.

To suppress talent at the sight of it is not the same as hiding the good and thwarting the excellent. Hiding carries the meaning of dark confinement; thwarting carries the misery of breaking and snapping. This goes a step further still. For to withhold praise where praise is due is precisely to suppress. Compared with the two preceding articles, the guilt seems somewhat lighter, yet the scrutiny is all the finer.

In the Warring States period Li Si and Han Fei of Zhou both studied under Xun Qing. Li Si knew in his own heart that his ability was not the equal of Han Fei's. When the King of Qin read Han Fei's book The Difficulties of Persuasion, he lamented that he could not meet the man. Later, when the King of Han sent Han Fei on a mission to Qin, the King of Qin spoke with him and was greatly pleased. Li Si feared he would be favored, slandered him, and had him thrown into prison, sending him poison. Han Fei wished to plead his own case but was not permitted an audience, and so died. Later Li Si was slandered by Zhao Gao and likewise wished to plead his case, and was not permitted. Those who understood took it as Heaven's way of returning like for like.

Sun Bian of the Song dynasty was a man of Meishan. He and Tang Jie and Wu Zhongfu had not known one another at first, but he admired their firmness and uprightness and therefore recommended them with all his strength, and they were promoted to censors. Zhang Xungong and Wen Lugong had never met, but hearing of their forthrightness, he recommended them at first sight, and afterward they went out as generals and came home as ministers. Yang Jingzhi loved talent and was just in heart; he once came to know a scholar of Jiangbiao named Xiang Si, and presented him with a poem: “Everywhere I see your poems, and all your poems are good; / and when I look upon your character, it surpasses your poems. / All my life I have not understood how to hide another's excellence: / wherever I go I tell everyone of Xiang Si.” These several gentlemen all advanced men of their own kind and encouraged and rewarded talent. Those who cannot seek out worthies for the state not only obstruct and suppress those who come after; they also cut off the seed by which the hundred families might be blessed. Alas! If one knows that to know men is the height of benevolence, then one knows that to envy the worthy is great evil.

According to the Code of the Mystic Capital, when offenses accumulate to two thousand seven hundred, that is one harm, and the family ought to produce a male or female shaman. If so, then to be born a shaman is already to be a man who made karma in a former age, and now to bury effigies and cast spells to harm others on another's behalf is only to deepen one's own hell. But there are those who give rise to the thought and have another do it; their guilt is even graver than the shaman's. If there be such, the king's law ought to behead them, and the yin law is stricter still.

Gongsun Chao, registrar of Wangwu in the Tang dynasty, died suddenly upon taking office. One day he appeared in a dream to the county magistrate and said: “I have a grievance and beg Your Honor to redress it. My allotted span was not yet due to end; I was killed by sorcery by my servants and concubines so that they might steal from me. My home is at Heyin. If Your Honor will secretly choose able officers and go with a warrant to arrest them, not one will slip the net. Under the eastern end of the hall's eaves, beneath the seventh roof-tile, there is a likeness of me made of tung wood, with nails driven all over it; it has already begun to change. The next day the magistrate did choose strong soldiers, took the warrant, and sent a letter to the magistrate of Heyin. They seized all the servants and concubines and searched beneath the hall's eaves. They found a human figure more than a foot long, its whole body covered with nails, the wood gradually turning to flesh; when struck it gave out a dull sound. All the grain and wheat Gongsun Chao had gathered had been stolen away. The magistrate then reported the matter to the prefecture, and all were executed. Now sorcery and baleful arts have their source mostly among women, maidservants, and concubines, for they wish to use them to grasp power and win favor, and their greed for gain is even more urgent than others'. People today should by all means set their own persons upright and keep their households in order, and guard well their doors, not allowing shamans and heterodox teachers to come and go. This is the way to stop it at the source. As for those in office, they too should issue strict orders for the search and arrest of such people, to cut off their traces. The merit of this is no small matter.

Every blade of grass and every tree is the living intent of the Creator. Gao Chai would not break a growing shoot, and Confucius praised him. The Buddha said that trees of many years are mostly dwelt in by ghosts and spirits, and must not be lightly felled; those who fell them often meet with calamity. If even to fell them is not permitted, how much less to kill them with poison?

Ru Yunqu of Taoyuan was venomous by nature. At odds with a neighbor, he secretly used poison to kill every one of the fruit trees the neighbor had planted. One day Ru came home from outside and in a daze saw lamplight flickering and soldiers in a crowded throng. He was bound by a crowd of attendants and dragged into the woods, where a god rebuked him, saying: “Trees and grasses are living things of Heaven above. How dare you take your anger out on them and kill them? It must be that your five organs are all out of balance.” He had the attendants cut open Ru's belly and take out his lungs and liver. Ru woke in terror and died of a pain in his heart and belly.

Chen Shi invited a geomancer to survey his ancestral grave. The man saw a great tree before the grave, planted at the edge of another family's plot, and took it for closing off the celestial heart; it must be removed, he said, if there was any hope of success in the examinations. He therefore urged Chen to buy fish and secretly pierce the tree with poison. Chen would not. He said: “Both families are seeking good fortune. And moreover it is a towering great tree; how could I bear to kill it?” Within a year the tree happened to be torn out by a great wind, and the celestial heart was suddenly clear. His son Chen Kui then passed the examinations in quick succession and became a censor.

This is different from being disrespectful to one's teacher. Disrespect is to be disrespectful without cause; this is to be angry and resentful because of correction and reproof. The way of the ancients in serving a teacher knew neither offense nor concealment: whatever teaching was given, one ought to receive it with an open heart and a gentle temper. How could one be angry and resentful? One who is angry and resentful must be a man of shallow virtue and no blessing.

Wang Huidao of the Ming dynasty was by nature quick and discerning; a book once passed before his eyes and he could recite it, and at eight he could write compositions. But in serving his teacher he was exceedingly arrogant. At the least thing that crossed his wishes he would turn his back on his teacher and curse him in anger. One day, sitting alone in his study, he suddenly yawned, and out of his mouth leaped a ghost, who pointed at Dao and said: “You were meant to come first in the whole empire. Because you are angry and resentful toward your teacher, the High God has struck your name from the register of emolument, and I too am leaving you from this moment.” With these words it vanished. When he sought out his old pages, he was utterly blank and could not recognize a single character.

Wei Zhao of the Eastern Han dynasty, as a boy, met Guo Linzong. He considered that a teacher of texts is easy to find, but a teacher of men is hard to meet, and so he begged to attend upon him, fetching water and sweeping. Linzong once fell ill and told Zhao to make gruel. When the gruel was ready Zhao brought it in, and Linzong cried out at him: “Making gruel for an elder, and you do not attend to it with care and respect, so that it cannot be eaten!” Zhao made the gruel again and brought it once more, and three times more he was shouted at, yet Zhao's countenance never changed. Linzong said: “At first I saw your face; from this day on I know your heart.”

Deng Zhi of the Song dynasty was a village schoolmaster, skilled at drawing students on and guiding them. Words of filial piety and fraternal duty never left his lips. He met people with sincerity and taught and guided them with all his heart. In the reign of Shenzong his eldest son Wan became a Hanlin academician, and his second son Ji and two grandsons all passed the imperial examination in the same list. Men all said this was the recompense for Deng Zhi's wholehearted teaching and guidance. Now a child born into a family of warmth and plenty may have his temperament transformed in a single day; yet there are those in whom arrogance and indulgence have become second nature, who easily fall into delusion and idleness. All depends on the man who is their teacher to lead and guide them with skillful means and bring them to awakening. Strive at it, strive at it.

Contradiction and defiance is likewise not the same as secret insult. The evil of secret insult is deep; the guilt of contradiction is open. In every word and deed, the least trace of non-compliance is contradiction. Now father and elder brother stand first among the five relations, and filial piety and fraternal duty come first in the human way. One ought to be respectful and compliant, with a gentle voice and a cheerful countenance. Even if a father has his partialities or an elder brother his encroachments, one should only accommodate and explain, and turn about and cultivate oneself. If by any chance he persists in delusion and will not turn back, one must still keep a gentle temper and a calm heart; in time things will naturally come into harmony. If one has the least breath of resentment, one will surely come to contradiction, and then one defies the relations and offends against principle, and the universe itself will not contain one.

Fei Hong of Ehu in the Ming dynasty, playing chess with a man of his own examination year, contended for the win and in jest slapped the man's cheek. The man of his year was displeased, and Hong repented and went day after day to beg pardon, but the man would not come out. Hong's father heard of it and was angry, and sealed up a stick and sent it to the capital residence, telling Hong to beat himself with it. Hong took his father's letter and the bamboo stick, went up into the man's hall, and beat himself three times. Only then did the man of his year come out, and clasping his head he wept. Hong said: “The fault was mine; why do you weep?” The man said: “You still have a father to discipline you. I seek one to discipline me and cannot find him.” They were as good friends as before. From this we may see that when one's parents are already gone, one can still be moved to grief by such an occasion; how much more, then, could one not bear to contradict them while they lived. But parents do not often live long. How painful, how painful.

Cui Xiaowei of the Later Wei dynasty served his elder brother Xiaofen, bending to the utmost in deference and compliance. In sitting and rising, in advancing and withdrawing, he did only as his brother commanded. Not a single coin or foot of cloth entered his private room. The wives of the household, too, loved one another, and this is a thing rarely seen in the common customs of today.

Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said: Men today are unfilial to their parents only because they will not lay a hand on their own hearts and think. Let them but consider from where this body came, and whither father and mother have gone. The new branch has risen, and the old root has withered. With coarse beans and water to gladden them, how can one ever repay? Then the filial heart will of itself ache. He also said: Men today are disrespectful to their elders only because they will not turn their hearts about and ask themselves. Let them but consider: in the vastness of the great Creator, how long is one out in the world? In the immensity of the human realm, how many are of one's own flesh? In childhood we mouthed and mouthed for each other; in old age we hold each other up. Then the bonds of feeling will of themselves grow sincere and earnest.

If people in the world will read the two cases of Fei and Cui, and Yan's words, carefully and with deep thought, then of themselves tears will stream in an instant, and their true nature will be laid out whole. Why then need the retribution of contradiction be listed at all?

blocks.text: The Collected Annotations, Lectures, and Case Records on the Tract of the Most High on Response and Retribution (Volume Four)

inline.s: 84. To seize by force and to extort by force. To delight in encroaching and in plundering.
85. To grow rich by plunder and pillage, and by cunning fraud to seek promotion.
86. To reward and punish unfairly. To carry ease and pleasure beyond due measure.
87. To treat those beneath one with harsh cruelty. To put others in fear.
88. To resent Heaven and lay blame on men. To rail at the wind and curse the rain.
89. To set men at odds and stir up litigation. To follow friends and factions in reckless pursuit.
90. To act on the words of wife and concubine. To disobey the instructions of father and mother.
91. Having gained the new, to forget the old. The mouth one thing, the heart another.
92. To be greedy and grasping after wealth. To deceive those above one. To invent evil words and slander and ruin the innocent.
93. To defame others and call it uprightness. To revile the gods and call it rectitude.
94. To cast off what is compliant and follow what is perverse. To turn one's back on kin and incline to strangers.
95. To call on Heaven and earth to witness base feelings. To invoke the gods to look upon filthy deeds. To give and then regret it. To borrow and not return.
96. To scheme and seek beyond one's lot. To strain one's strength to lay on more.
97. To carry lust and desire beyond due measure.
98. A heart of poison and a face of kindness. To feed men filthy food. By heterodox ways to delude the crowd.
99. Short foot and narrow measure. Light scales and small pints. To mix the false in with the true. To take wicked profit.
100. To press the good down into baseness. To cheat and deceive the foolish.
101. To be greedy without satiety. To curse and swear in order to prove oneself right.
102. To be addicted to wine and to rebel against order.
103. Flesh and blood quarrelling in anger. Men not loyal and good. Women not gentle and compliant.
104. To live without harmony in one's household. To show no respect to one's elders by marriage.
105. Always fond of boasting. Constantly given to envy and jealousy.
106. To be without principle toward wife and children. To fail in courtesy toward one's husband's parents.
107. To slight and neglect the spirits of the departed. To disobey and defy the commands of those above one.
108. To do what is of no benefit. To harbor a heart turned elsewhere.
109. To curse oneself and to curse others. To be partial in hatred and partial in love.
110. To step over wells and over hearths. To step over food and over people.
111. To destroy children and procure abortions. To go much in secret and crooked ways.

112. On the last day of the month and at the year's end, to sing and dance. On the first day of the month, to wail and rage. To spit, snivel, and urinate facing north. To chant and weep facing the hearth.
113. Again, to light incense with the hearth fire. To cook food with filthy firewood. To rise at night and go about naked. To carry out executions on the eight festival days.
114. To spit at shooting stars. To point at the rainbow. To point at the three lights at random. To gaze long at the sun and moon.
115. In the spring months to burn the fields for hunting. To revile and curse facing north. To kill tortoises and strike snakes without cause.

116. For sins such as these, the Master of Destinies takes away from a man's span of years according to the weight of each. When the span is exhausted, he dies; and if guilt remains after death, it passes on to sons and grandsons.

117. Again, those who take men's wealth by violence — the reckoning is made against their wives, children, and household, until it comes to death and loss. If they do not die, then there are flood and fire, robbers and thieves, lost and vanished goods, illness and slander and all such things, to make up the value of what was wrongly taken.
118. Again, those who wrongfully kill men are but exchanging the blade and the weapon to kill one another.

119. Those who take wealth that is not rightfully theirs are like men who save themselves from hunger with tainted meat, or quench their thirst with poisoned wine: it is not that they are not briefly filled, but death comes upon them too.

120. Now when the heart gives rise to good, though the good be not yet done, the auspicious spirits already follow after. Or when the heart gives rise to evil, though the evil be not yet done, the baleful spirits already follow

121. If there be one who has formerly done evil and afterward repents and reforms, does no evil at all, and practices every good, then in the course of time he will surely obtain auspicious blessing. This is what is meant by turning calamity into fortune.
after him.

122. Therefore the auspicious man — his speech good, his sight good, his conduct good — has three goods in a day; in three years Heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious man — his speech evil, his sight evil, his conduct evil — has three evils in a day; in three years Heaven will surely send down calamity upon him. Why then does one not strive and practice it?

To insist on obtaining what by one's lot one ought not to have is called force. To make others supply me is called taking. To beg of others on my own account is called soliciting. To take secretly by cunning scheme is called encroaching. To take openly by power is called plundering. What is gotten in such ways a man can hardly digest; he will surely lose along with it what he had before.

Zheng Xuan said: I have observed that money is a thing all men love alike and all contend for of necessity. Flesh and blood start feuds because of it, officials ruin their names through it, merchants lose their lives for it, and the marketplace takes it as occasion to fight and slaughter. It comes and goes suddenly; in a flash one is noble, in a flash poor. Of those it ensnares for a whole lifetime, for the most part it blesses few and harms many. I have often looked closely at its shape: on the side of gold it bears a spear — truly a thing that kills men, and men do not awaken. Alas, money, money! In my poverty I begged you to keep me alive and could not get you; I was helpless before you. And in my poverty, if you would kill me, you cannot do that either; how then can you do anything to me?

Duke Zhao Xiong, while still of low estate, was utterly poor. His mother was alive, and he had nothing with which to get through the year; husband and wife wept face to face. The next day, sweeping the ground, he picked up a silver ingot weighing twenty-five ounces, and so was able to keep going a little. Later he rose to the office of prime minister. By custom he was due a hundred ingots of silver, and when he received them one was missing. He was about to question the treasury clerk, when in a dream at night a god said to him: “On such-and-such a day of such-and-such a month, Your Excellency borrowed one ingot in advance.” Now if wealth is in one's destiny, yet the time of good fortune has not come, it still cannot be brought about by force; how much less may one seize by force what one was never due at all?

Zhao the Minister of Jiangxi lived near Chang the provincial graduate. Chang had a garden of great elegance, and Zhao schemed in a hundred ways to force it from him. Chang drew up a deed and gave it to Zhao, writing a poem on the back: “North and south, east and west, everywhere is my pavilion; / contrivance has never yet been true. / What is it all, this turning rain to cloud and back? / The clear wind and bright moon look on coldly at men. / The Orchid Pavilion gathering is no longer of Jin; / the flower spirits of the peach grotto laugh at Qin as well. / The garden is the host and I am but the guest — / may I ask, sir, how many more springs have you?” When Zhao received the poem he repented, begged pardon, and dared not accept it. Chang afterward rose to high examination honors. Mr. Chang moved men by virtue, and Mr. Zhao was brave in repenting of his fault. Both are rare in these days.

A certain Yang of Kunshan was sitting one day at his gate when he saw a woman pass by and drop a silver hairpin on the paving stones of the street, which rang out as it struck. He hurried to look, and saw an earthworm. He hesitated over it a long while. Suddenly a man came by and picked it up. Old Yang cried out in a loud voice: “That is the hairpin I dropped!” The man knew it was a falsehood and went straight on. Old Yang would not let him go, and the man took out two fen of silver, buying fish with half and giving the other half to him with the words: “Old man, do not keep pestering. Take this silver and buy wine; boil the fish and make an evening of it.” Old Yang went home and had his daughter-in-law boil the fish. While the wine was warming, the neighbor's cat suddenly snatched the fish and ran; the daughter-in-law struck at it with a stick and in the confusion the wine was overturned and the dish holding the fish was broken with it. Now the hairpin had turned into an earthworm — one might well have taken the lesson. Yet he still extorted it by force. Could he eat it? Alas, what a greedy fellow! Alas, what a man of thin fate! If small matters are thus, one may know what the great ones are.

In Yin County there was a man surnamed Lu, cunning and rich. A neighbor of his, the Zheng family, had an estate, and Lu by secret scheming encroached on it and got it. He tore down their dwelling to make halls and gardens, and all that remained was one fine tree. Later Lu had a son, who at five was mute and could not speak. Then one day the boy pointed at the tree and said: “Tree, are you still here?” The family was greatly alarmed, and after that he was mute again. They tried every means to cure him, but he never uttered a sound. When he grew up he was dissipated and arrogant, and only died when the family fortune was exhausted. Men said he was the rebirth of the man of the Zheng family.

Wang Sheng of the Southern Capital in the Ming dynasty was greedy and mean by nature. An elder of his clan died without heirs, though there was already one adopted to succeed him. Wang Sheng, seeing how rich the family was, tried by force to seize the succession. The lawsuit went on for several years, and when the presiding official upheld public justice and gave him a slight rebuff, he reviled and slandered him without cease. That year he sat for the autumn examination, and it happened that the very official was appointed as an examiner. He had already selected Wang Sheng's paper as first when he opened it and saw the name — it was the man who had tried to seize the succession. He flung it aside and threw it out.

What is called plunder — were it not for the fires of war, how could it exist? Yet when an official in office swallows and flays the common people, or secretly steals from the public coffers, or when the powerful lend money at heavy interest, all of this is plunder. To grow rich by such means always comes out of broken homes and scattered families; amid the wife's weeping and the children's sobbing, how could one enjoy it in peace? Have you not heard the saying about the pu-man, the “fling-full”? The History of the Han calls it hou; it is what today we call the “muffled gourd.” It is made of earthenware with a slot on top, into which one may put things but out of which they cannot come. Men use it to store coins, and when it is full they smash it and take the money — hence the name “fling-full.” While they are gathering, they fear only that it will not be full; when at last the money fills it, it is smashed and broken and that is the end. The jar is broken and the money gone, and both are emptiness. Much stored up and heavily lost — what difference is there from this?

Wen Yanbo, Duke Lu of the Song dynasty, went out to govern Chang'an. One day he came to the Benniu weir, where a weir ox spoke in human speech, saying: “Wen Yanbo and I were colleagues in office for twenty years. With what face shall I meet him today?” The weir guard reported it, and the duke had the ox brought to him. When the ox came it knelt on the ground and dropped its head, and its tears fell like rain. The duke sighed greatly and said: “This man stole and plundered public money all his life; now he has gotten this retribution.” He therefore ordered the household treasury to pay out twenty strings of cash to increase its fodder. Now public money is what the people supply; to become an ox and build a weir is to repay the people. Whoever reads this should think on it.

Dai Wen was greedy by nature. Whenever he lent money to others, he took back double interest, and if repayment was a little late he went in person to press for it. For larger debts he took fields, houses, and sons and daughters; for smaller ones, clothing, ornaments, and livestock — all were stripped bare. When he died, he was born into a neighbor's house as an ox, with white hair on its flank forming the two characters “Dai Wen.” The neighbors all hired it to plow, and one who had once been plundered by him drove it cruelly.

An oil-seller of Suzhou went to a great household and saw a little child of five with a pearl cap and a golden lock. He conceived an evil thought, carried the child off to a secluded place, and killed him, and so suddenly grew rich. He had a son who resembled exactly the child he had killed, and he greatly loathed him. When the boy was five, the oil-seller happened to fall asleep in the heat of summer, and the child drew the silver hairpin from his topknot and in play jabbed it into his chest. The man, thinking it a bluebottle fly, raised his hand and slapped at it, and the pin passed through his chest and he died. From this we see that those who today deck out their children in gold and pearls should also be careful and take warning.

Once a noble man enters the ranks of office, he ought to take loyalty, uprightness, public spirit, and integrity as his own proper business. But today men seek promotion by cunning fraud, and their mind and craft are utterly crooked. Place such a man in the court, and he will surely not be loyal and public-spirited; send him out to govern the people, and how could he be honest and clean? Therefore the Most High specially warns against it. And moreover, whether a man's merit and fame in life come early or late is settled the moment he is born; even if he toils and schemes his whole life, he adds not a hair's breadth, and only supplies men of understanding with laughter and shame and earns the rebuke of gods and spirits.

In the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Liu Song dynasty, Dai Faxing, Dai Mingbao, and Chao Shangzhi held power, and their weight was felt in the world; whatever they recommended was carried out without fail. Gu Jizhi alone would not bend his will to them. He once said: “What a man receives by decree has its fixed portion and cannot be shifted by wit or strength. One should only revere oneself and keep to the Way. To scheme cunningly after a lucky chance is only to lose what one should keep. What has it to do with gain or loss?” Someone who observed this asked me: “Then why is it that men today often obtain office by clever contrivance?” I answered: “That too is destiny. Nevertheless, to take game by an underhand shot is a thing a noble man will surely not do.”

In the yisi year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, a certain Ji of Shanyin was appointed to be the relay station officer of Longjiang Bridge in Yunnan. He dreaded the distance and did not wish to go. There was a wine-selling commoner named Zhou whose household was comfortably off, and Ji had once lodged in his house. He said to him: “Give me two hundred pieces of silver, and I will hand over to you my commission.” Zhou's heart was set on it; he gave the money and got the commission. When he took up the post, it happened that the provincial military governor had once known him, and constantly assigned him fine commissions, so that in five years he gained several thousand pieces of silver. Zhou, his wish now fulfilled, pleaded illness and went home. As for this Mr. Ji, after getting the money he changed his name once more and went to work in the Ministry of Personnel. By the time Zhou returned home, Ji was due for an appointment again. One night, going to the privy, he saw two servants in blue speaking together: “What office is this man to have?” The answer came: “Relay station officer of Longjiang Bridge.” With these words they vanished. When he went to the selection, he got Longjiang Bridge again. He had scarcely taken up the post when the rebellion of Wu broke out, and where he ended no one knows.

Qian Bangqi of Dantu in the Qing dynasty said: However great a man's powers of working the heavens, in the end how can he contend with the fixed decree? Only in the one matter of hidden merit can the fixed decree surely be turned back. Do it yesterday and it takes effect today; do it in the morning and it takes effect by evening. Of all retributions the hidden ones are the swiftest; the divine mirror is exceedingly clear. This is the road with no shortcut to match it. Let a man of intention but try it once, and he will know.

To err on the side of lightness or on the side of heaviness, to go astray by a single fraction, is unfairness. When public justice is not kept, men's hearts will not submit. Not only is there no way to honor merit and punish guilt; it is rather enough to pile up resentment and invite calamity.

Zhuge Kongming of Shu-Han said: “My heart is a balance; it cannot weigh light or heavy for any man.” Chen Shou praised him, saying: “Those who were wholly loyal and beneficial to the times he rewarded even if they were his enemies; those who broke the law and were negligent he punished even if they were his kin. Those who submitted to their guilt and gave up their true feelings he released even though their crime was heavy; those who used specious words and cunning adornment he put to death even though the matter was light.” Hence at that time all the generals gave their lives to his orders, and even such a restless man as Wei Yan was quietly submissive and had no word of dissent. Li Ping and Liao Li were dismissed and banished for life, yet bore no resentment. Let those who preside over reward and punishment take their lesson from this.

Ease and pleasure are what all men desire alike. The Book of Rites says: “Pleasure must not be carried to the extreme; desire must not be indulged.” The Discourses of the States says: “When the people toil they think of goodness; when at ease they think of license” — that is, it does not wish men to be at ease. Mencius says: “Men are born in sorrow and die in ease” — that is, it does not wish men to take their pleasure. How much less, then, should one pass due measure? Yet the great roots of ease and pleasure in this world are nothing more than wine, lust, wealth, and temper. A man today who is fond of wine will not heed his own body; who loves beauty will not heed his illness; who covets wealth will not heed his kin; who gives way to temper will not heed his life. Before they come upon the occasion, all such men can reason themselves free and can even advise others; but when the circumstance is before them they grow dim and commit it themselves. It is only that they see through it and yet cannot bear it. If one could truly grasp the four words “ease and pleasure beyond due measure,” then habitual feelings could be changed and familiar circumstances forgotten, and one could reach a state of few desires and a clear heart, and stand with head to heaven and feet on earth.

The monk Zhigong, discussing the matter of pleasure with Emperor Wu of Liang, asked the emperor to produce several condemned criminals as a test. He then commanded the prisoners each to carry a cup filled to the brim with water and walk around the hall below, warning them: “If not a drop of the water spills, your death will be pardoned.” This done, he had music played to stir their hearts. After a long while he looked at them, and not one had spilled a single drop. The emperor sighed and said: “Did you hear the music?” They answered: “We did not hear it.” The master said: “They were in fear of death, dreading only that the water would spill; how could they hear the music? If a man could thus constantly harbor fear, then the mind of ease and pleasure would of course not arise.”

Yu Tieqiao said: The diligence of carrying bricks and the carefulness of one treading on ice or standing at a precipice — the great men and sages and worthies were all like this. What manner of man am I, that I should dare to be at ease and extravagant? The Book of Changes says: “The movement of Heaven is strong; the noble man strengthens himself without cease.” It is only that men have no ambition to strengthen themselves, and so, if only there is no urgent matter touching their own persons, they think at once of passing the day at their ease. But if one has the ambition to strengthen himself, then the things he ought to do are endless, and he truly finds the days too few. He has no leisure for pleasure and dares not be idle.

Fan Zhongyan, Duke Wenzheng of the Song dynasty, said: “Every night when I go to bed I reckon up the cost of the day's food and support and compare it with the work I have done by day. If they match, I sleep soundly and deeply with no further shame. If by any chance they do not, I cannot rest my head on the pillow all night.”

Sima Guang, Duke Wenguo of the Song dynasty, said: When my late father was a prefectural judge, when guests came he set out wine, sometimes three rounds, sometimes five, but never more than seven. The wine was bought in the market; the fruit was only pears, chestnuts, dates, and persimmons; the dishes were only dried meat, minced meat, vegetable soup; the vessels were of porcelain, lacquer, bamboo, and wood. At that time all the scholar-officials did the same, and no one thought it wrong.

Qiu Tairan of the Song dynasty, serving as governor of Siming, was on good terms with a subordinate official. One day he asked him the amount of his daily expenses, and the man answered that for a household of ten mouths he used a thousand cash a day. Tairan said: “What need for so much?” He answered: “In the morning I set out a little meat; in the evening, vegetable soup.” Tairan said in astonishment: “I am the prefect, and ordinarily I eat vegetables. You eat meat every day. You are certainly no honest man.” And he kept his distance from him.

In the Yuan dynasty there were two students of the Imperial College, born in the same year, month, day, and hour, who passed the provincial examination together and on the same day were appointed to office: one was made professor of Ezhou, the other professor of Huangzhou. Not long after, the one at Huangzhou died, and the one at Ezhou was greatly afraid; he settled his affairs after death, but after several days he had not died. So he prepared gifts and went to offer condolences. He wept, saying: “You and I were born in the same year, month, day, and hour, and our paths in life were the same. Now you have gone before me. If I were to die now, I would be seven days behind you. If your spirit has awareness, you should entrust me with a dream and tell me the reason.” That night he dreamed that the man of Huangzhou told him: “You are frugal in all things, and so you live long. I carried my enjoyments beyond due measure, and so my span was shortened.”

The rich man Yu of the Liang dynasty built a high tower overlooking the great road, and day and evening he sang and feasted and played chess upon it with his beauties. When a player won he covered his mouth and laughed. It happened that three travelers passed below the tower, and a kite dropped a rotten rat upon one of them. The traveler raised his head, and it was just at the moment of the laughter. He was furious and said: “The Yu family have had their wealth and pleasure long enough. I have not encroached on them; why do they insult me?” So he gathered a crowd and destroyed the family. Gu Xichou said: Even if the high tower did not overlook the great road, there would still be strange calamities. This is what is meant by the calamity of arrogance and extravagance; the disasters are not of one kind. Yet among the calamities of arrogance and extravagance, none is fiercer or swifter than woman's beauty, and it should be the first thing warned against. A plain-speaking rustic once said: “A skin wrapping blood and flesh and filth, / yet it forces itself into coquetry to delude and bewitch men. / Through the ages many a hero has fallen by this; / in a hundred years all alike become dust in one pit.” If a man can grasp this principle, and likewise hold in reverence and keep the warnings in the annotations on “seeing another's beauty and giving rise to a private thought” and on “carrying lust beyond due measure,” then form and emptiness will both be empty, and he will scarcely be harmed by ease and pleasure.

To be cruel and tyrannical toward the officials and people while in high station, or at home to flog and beat servants and bondmaids beyond measure — both are harsh cruelty. Cruelty toward those below while in high station has been fully spoken of in the course of this book, and so here I set out in detail only the matter of treating those below one at home.

The Buddha told Shijialuoyue: In dealing with their slaves and servants, all people of the world should observe five things. First, they should first know their hunger and thirst, their cold and heat, and only then set them to work. Second, when they are ill, one should have them treated. Third, one must not use the whip at random; one should ask whether the matter is true or false, and only then reprove and correct. What can be forgiven, forgive; what cannot be forgiven, instruct and correct. Fourth, if they have a little private property, one must not seize it. Fifth, in giving out goods and clothing, one should make them equal and must not be partial or crooked. The Yuan Family Precepts for the World says: Servants and those below one are mostly dull by nature and often err in their work; they are also forgetful by nature, so that when one entrusts a matter to them they remember nothing of it. They are also stubborn by nature, always thinking themselves right; and perverse by nature, quick to answer back and unable to tell high from low. Every head of a household, in giving orders, should deal with them generously, teach them much, and not be angry. Then the master's own heart will feel at peace. Even if they commit a fault and must be corrected, one should calmly question and reprove them; and once they have been reproved, when next one calls and commands them, one's countenance should be as usual, and then there will be no further trouble. As for the women, who are narrow and obstinate by temper, the head of the household should constantly instruct and guide them; and the young men of the house should not be permitted to beat those below them at will; if there is a matter, they should have it reported to the head of the household. But as for the stubborn, violent, and wicked, one should send them away skillfully and must not be too severe, for fear such men harbor resentment and do evil.

The Poem on Selling a Son says: “I raised you like a phoenix chick; / when the year is lean, what are you worth? / Toil on and take good care of yourself — / no longer are you at your mother's side.” It also says: “I have wept out all the blood in my eyes / and sprinkled it on the clothes you wear. / If the bond of karma is not yet severed, / I still hope to see you return in a dream.”

Yu Tieqiao said: In governing those below one, harsh cruelty is of course unbearable, but indulgence is especially unfitting. How often one sees in the houses of great officials and nobles how the overbearing slaves and violent servants are honored as though they were emperors of Heaven: going out, they ride fierce horses in fresh silks; coming in, they gamble and drink. Guests may come to the gate and they sit and pay no courtesy; kinsmen may call and they refuse to announce them. Thus the strong depart in anger and the weak go away swallowing their hatred. They go so far as to seize on pretexts to stir up trouble and to use their masters' power to extort money, while the master never hears of it at all. And so the crowd rebels and kin are estranged, friends become enemies and men bear grudges — one does not know how many by then. Be careful.

Tao Yuanming of the Jin dynasty admonished his sons, saying: “The tasks of your mornings and evenings are hard enough to provide for yourselves. Now I send you this servant to help you with the labor of gathering firewood and water. He too is a man's son; treat him well.”

The wife of Yang Wanli of the Song dynasty, of the Chengzhai household, was over seventy. In the depth of every winter she would rise early and go to the kitchen and with her own hands make a whole cauldron of gruel, which she gave out to all the bondservants before they were made to serve. Her son Dongshan said: “The weather is cold; why torment yourself like this?” The lady said: “Bondservants too are men's sons. In the cold of early morning they must have a little fire in their chests before they can serve.”
